summary:
Marswalk is a habitat-to-helmet planning and navigation prototype for future human exploration of Mars. We developed a mission-control console, a terrain-aware route engine, and an astronaut visor interface (demonstrated today as a phone AR navigator) that turn NASA mission data into actionable exploration plans. Using real terrain and imagery from Gale crater, Marswalk evaluates science stops against slope, estimated exertion, daylight, communication coverage, and return-to-shelter constraints. The habitat operator reviews and confirms a route, then sends it to the visor, which retains navigation guidance when the local connection fails.

Marswalk addresses the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge by connecting planetary maps to the decisions an exploration crew must make: where to go, what science to prioritize, and when to return. Its importance lies in demonstrating local decision support for missions where immediate help from Earth is unavailable. Every major constraint exposes its evidence or assumptions, making the prototype useful for education, mission-design discussions, and further research.
details:
We developed three connected components: a habitat planning console, a shared route-planning engine, and a browser-based astronaut visor, demonstrated on a phone in AR.

A Python pipeline converts NASA mission data into downloadable site packs containing elevation, imagery, slope, terrain roughness, thermal-inertia context, rover locations, and science stations. The main demonstration covers a five-kilometre-square region of Gale crater near Mount Sharp. Maps use Mars-specific coordinates and distances.

The habitat console lets an operator choose an exploration base and science objectives, inspect terrain, generate a route, and understand why particular destinations are excluded. The planner considers outward travel and the return journey, including estimated metabolic effort, suit heat limits, emergency walking reserves, daylight, shelter access, and terrain-based communication visibility. Its reports identify the constraints limiting an excursion and the science objectives it can cover.

Once approved, a compact, digitally signed route package is transmitted to the visor. The astronaut interface displays direction, distance, station tasks, rover photographs, and remaining return margins. Stored route information supports continued guidance during simulated communication loss. Demonstration controls introduce hazards, solar-particle-event scenarios, and shortened excursions to explore replanning.

The creative contribution is the connection between scientific evidence, operational planning, and the astronaut’s immediate experience. Users can watch the reachable area shrink as constraints are applied, then follow the resulting plan through a second interface. This makes the consequences of terrain, base placement, and limited resources visible.

We used TypeScript, React, Node.js, Hono, WebSockets, OpenLayers, and Python. Rasterio/GDAL, NumPy, SciPy, and related tools process planetary rasters. Vitest, Playwright, and Python checks support testing. The demonstration runs on ordinary computers and browsers; the visor is a software prototype, not certified helmet hardware. Claude Code assisted development under team direction, as disclosed in the repository.

Our team considered delayed communications, intermittent connectivity, bandwidth, readable displays, scientific value, coordinate accuracy, data provenance, and uncertainty. We compared selected radiation and metabolic calculations with published research. These are reproduction and calibration exercises: human performance at Mars gravity remains an extrapolation, orbital imagery cannot resolve every foot-level hazard, and terrain shielding is not equivalent to a protective shelter.

Results (simulation, Gale crater): a slope-only planner broke at least one EVA constraint in 199 of 200 simulated walks. Marswalk re-plans mid-walk in a median of 8.3 ms on a laptop. Its walking model has a 10.6% mean error against NASA suited-walking data at 0.22–0.32 g. An independently written checker agreed with its verdicts on 23 of 24 walks, and staging from a pressurized rover turned an infeasible habitat walk into a six-stop plan. Method and limits are in our 17-page research paper: https://github.com/NASASpaceHacks/NASASpaceHacks2026/blob/main/docs/paper/marswalk-paper.pdf. The helmet visor is the end goal; today it is demonstrated as a phone AR navigator. Its proposed hardware (LCoS waveguide display, boot IMUs, and camera-to-orbital-map matching using Mars Global Localization) is a concept study and has not been built.
